extracted.intended_audience: journalists, Reuters reporters, editors and copy-editors
extracted.subtask_short: reuters style guide for news writing
extracted.subtask_description: A newsroom style and usage guide for Reuters journalists and editors covering word choice, punctuation, capitalization, names, reporting practice and other copyediting conventions for news stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periods and quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Periods (full points, full stops) go inside quotation marks unless it is a broken quote, i.e. a phrase or a single word, in which case they go outside the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use periods inside quotes for complete-sentence quotations; place outside for broken quotes or when the quotation is the final part of the sentence. See also detailed rules under 'quotations' about commas and full stops with quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'period of time'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use one word or the other, not both together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid tautological or redundant pairings such as 'period of time' when a single word will do.

rubrics_metrics.name: perk
rubrics_metrics.description: Shortened form of perquisite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain as a fringe benefit when using the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persian (language name)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic name for the language spoken in Iran, Tajikistan and northern Afghanistan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although locally known as Farsi, Tajik and Dari, 'Persian' is the preferred overall name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persian Gulf
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred terminology for the body of water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'Gulf' as shorthand where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: person, people
rubrics_metrics.description: Person is singular and people is plural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use 'persons'. Use 'people' for plural references.

rubrics_metrics.name: personal / personally / personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal or personally (meaning private or individual) is almost always unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid redundancy (e.g., 'He personally took his personal belongings'). For 'personnel' use 'people', 'staff' or 'workers' where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: personal names
rubrics_metrics.description: Check names repeatedly; use given name and surname at first identification and surname alone on second reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never presume spelling; use initials only if given name not available or person prefers initials; repeat odd-looking given names at first reference; use he/she at second reference when gender is unclear; follow same rules in sports stories; write 'declined to be identified' not 'declined to be named'.

rubrics_metrics.name: persuade vs convince
rubrics_metrics.description: You persuade people to do something, convince them of something or that something is the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never write 'convince to'. Use 'persuade' for getting someone to act and 'convince' for changing belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: petrol bomb terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition: a bottle of petrol with a petrol-soaked rag set alight and thrown to cause an explosion on impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use 'Molotov cocktail'.

rubrics_metrics.name: PGA
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviation usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PGA stands for Professional Golfers’ Association.

rubrics_metrics.name: phase vs faze
rubrics_metrics.description: Phase is a stage in growth or development; faze is to worry or disturb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct word to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: phenomenon / phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Phenomena is the plural; do not use 'phenomenal' if you mean extraordinary or remarkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'phenomenal' only in its proper senses, not simply as a synonym for big or remarkable.

rubrics_metrics.name: pigeonhole
rubrics_metrics.description: Both noun and verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriately as either part of speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: pilots / crew wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Military aircraft other than strategic bombers and transports normally carry only one pilot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting incidents involving fighter-bombers and similar craft, write 'the two crew' not 'the two pilots'.

rubrics_metrics.name: pileup noun/verb
rubrics_metrics.description: One word as a noun, two words as a verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'pileup' (noun) and 'pile up' (verb).

rubrics_metrics.name: PIN
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal identification number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'PIN number' as tautologous.

rubrics_metrics.name: pious
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid describing someone as 'a pious Muslim' or 'a pious Christian'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'practising' instead of 'pious'.

rubrics_metrics.name: plan ahead
rubrics_metrics.description: Use shorter phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'plan' rather than 'plan ahead'.

rubrics_metrics.name: plane
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'aircraft' for an airplane; but 'higher plane' is acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'plane' when 'aircraft' is clearer, except in figurative/higher-plane uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: planets capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalise the names of planets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow standard capitalization for proper planetary names.

rubrics_metrics.name: plea bargain noun/verb
rubrics_metrics.description: Plea bargain is the noun; plea-bargain is the verb used only intransitively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The verb is not used transitively (do not write 'The lawyer plea-bargained the case').

rubrics_metrics.name: plead / pleaded
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'pleaded' rather than the legalese 'pled'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer standard English 'pleaded'.

rubrics_metrics.name: PLO abbreviation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: PLO refers to Palestine Liberation Organisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PLO is acceptable on first reference; spell out in a subsequent reference. (Give full name at appropriate point if necessary.)

rubrics_metrics.name: plummet (market reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'plummet' in market reports unless it is a precipitous decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 2-percent fall is not a plummet; reserve strong verbs for dramatic moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: p.m. time formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Time example formatting: e.g. 3 p.m. or 3:45 p.m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lower-case with periods for a.m./p.m. (per Reuters guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: podium vs lectern/dais
rubrics_metrics.description: A speaker stands behind a lectern (a stand for notes) on a podium and in a pulpit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'lectern' for the stand for notes; 'podium' denotes the raised platform; several speakers can fit on a dais/rostrum/platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: poem title capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalise every word in the title apart from conjunctions, articles, particles and short prepositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner', 'Elegy in a Country Churchyard', 'The Waste Land'.

rubrics_metrics.name: point-blank hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Note hyphen: 'point-blank'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyphenate as shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid 'pointed out' for contentious statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'pointed out' if the statement is contentious since it suggests the writer accepts it as fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'said' for neutral attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: police terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'police officers', not 'policemen'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer gender-neutral terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: policymakers compound
rubrics_metrics.description: One word: 'policymakers'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use closed form.

rubrics_metrics.name: political parties capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of political parties and movements with a specific doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lower case for non-specific references and lower case for political philosophies (communism, communist) unless derived from a proper noun (Marxism). Examples given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pope capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize only as a title before a name; use lower case when referring to 'the pope'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See religious titles guidance for consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: populace usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'populace' to mean the common folk, not the population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose more precise words if you mean 'population'.

rubrics_metrics.name: pour vs pore
rubrics_metrics.description: Pour liquid; pore over maps and documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse the two homophones.

rubrics_metrics.name: port and starboard usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Port is left, starboard right in nautical parlance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'left' and 'right' for general readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portuguese names
rubrics_metrics.description: Portuguese and Brazilians include family names of both father and mother; the mother's name normally comes before the father's and both are normally retained at second reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At second reference either or both names may be used; when one is used it is typically the patronymic (the last name).

rubrics_metrics.name: posh
rubrics_metrics.description: Slang — avoid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clearer descriptors.

rubrics_metrics.name: positive (word choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'positive' as a synonym for good or fruitful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose more precise adjectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: postmarket
rubrics_metrics.description: One word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use closed form 'postmarket'.

rubrics_metrics.name: post mortem usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Needs the word 'examination' afterwards — a post mortem examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By itself 'post mortem' means 'after death'.

rubrics_metrics.name: postpone vs cancel
rubrics_metrics.description: Events called off but held later are postponed; only events scrapped completely are cancelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the new date if possible. Note American style spellings: cancel, canceled, canceling vs cancellation.

rubrics_metrics.name: postwar hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: No hyphen: 'postwar'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use closed form.

rubrics_metrics.name: pound abbreviation and conversions
rubrics_metrics.description: The abbreviation lb (no full stop) is acceptable in singular and plural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversion guidance: to grams multiply by 454 precisely; to kg multiply by 0.454; rough conversions given in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: pound sign usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'pounds' rather than the '£' sign to denote sums in sterling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 420 (followed by context).

rubrics_metrics.name: practice / practise
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice is the noun, practise the verb (British). In American style 'practice' is both noun and verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow regional spelling conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: prefix hyphenation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule do not hyphenate prefixes; exceptions: prefix ends in a vowel and following word starts with same vowel (pre-eminence, pre-establish), Cooperate/coordinate exceptions, hyphenate when the following element is capitalised (trans-Panamanian).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transatlantic and transpacific are exceptions; hyphenate pre- or re- before e (pre-empt).

rubrics_metrics.name: precautionary measure phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'precaution' alone instead of 'precautionary measure'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid verbosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: precondition tautology
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'precondition' as tautological; 'condition' is enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simpler wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: pre-dawn cliché
rubrics_metrics.description: Although technically correct for shortly before dawn, 'pre-dawn' is a cliché to avoid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use it to mean merely that something happened during the night.

rubrics_metrics.name: predominant / predominantly
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'predominant'/'predominantly' rather than 'predominate'/'predominately'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct adjective/adverb forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: premarket
rubrics_metrics.description: One word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use closed form 'premarket'.

rubrics_metrics.name: premier vs prime minister
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'premier' for heads of government in states that are part of a larger political entity; reserve 'prime minister' for heads of government of sovereign states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Premier' may be used for brevity in a headline.

rubrics_metrics.name: premiere definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The debut, opening or first showing of a TV show or film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: premier league capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The English premier league is not capitalised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower case as shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: premise / premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Premises (property) is always plural; a premise is a proposition supporting an argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer exact descriptions (the house, the factory) and avoid legalistic wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: pre-owned
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'second-hand' not 'pre-owned'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer standard terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: preplanned tautology
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'preplanned' as tautological; 'planned' is enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excise redundant prefixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: prepositional phrases verbosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases that start and end with a preposition are usually verbose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid expressions like 'in order to', 'in accordance with', 'at this moment', 'in respect to', 'in receipt of', 'with a view to', 'in connection with', 'in the wake of', 'apprehension as to the outcome'; prefer concise alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: prescribe vs proscribe
rubrics_metrics.description: Prescribe is to set down as an order; proscribe is to prohibit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct verb to avoid reversing meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: presently
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'presently' to mean 'in a short time' or 'soon', rather than 'now' or 'at present'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid redundant usages of 'present' and 'presently' when they mean 'now'.

rubrics_metrics.name: President capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'President' only when a formal title immediately precedes a name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower case otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidents Day punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: No apostrophe: Presidents Day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unofficial holiday name; follow this spelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: presidency
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower case 'presidency'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lower case in general references.

rubrics_metrics.name: press conference phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'news conference' unless broadcast journalists, photographers and camera operators have been excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'news conference' in general reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: press reports sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: When picking up newspaper, radio or television reports, name the source; do not refer just to 'press reports'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting a news report does not absolve journalists from responsibility for accuracy and balance. Make every effort to check a pick-up; insert relevant background and indicate the political stance, reliability and potential for bias of the source.

rubrics_metrics.name: pressurise
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'press' or 'pressure' unless speaking of industrial processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simpler words.

rubrics_metrics.name: prestigious
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'prestigious' as a pompous and often tautological word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If something is prestigious or famous, the copy need not say so.

rubrics_metrics.name: pretax
rubrics_metrics.description: One word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use closed form 'pretax'.

rubrics_metrics.name: pretence vs pretext
rubrics_metrics.description: A pretence is a false show or sham; a pretext is an ostensible motive put forward to conceal the real one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct noun to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: prevaricate vs procrastinate
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevaricate means to mislead or lie; procrastinate means to delay or defer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse the verbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: prime minister capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the title when it immediately precedes the person’s name; otherwise use lower case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'French Prime Minister Jacques Dupont'; 'the French prime minister'.

rubrics_metrics.name: prime rate definition (US)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States the prime rate is a benchmark reference for determining interest rates on short-term loans to high-quality large borrowers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often used erroneously; actual bank lending rates may be higher or lower.

rubrics_metrics.name: principal vs principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle is always a noun meaning a fundamental basis or truth; principal can be an adjective meaning chief or a noun meaning chief person or capital sum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct word to avoid common error.

rubrics_metrics.name: prior to
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'before' instead of 'prior to'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor simpler prepositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: prise apart
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'prise apart', not 'prize'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for common misspellings.

rubrics_metrics.name: prison officers term
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'prison officers', not 'jailers' or 'warders'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the correct institutional term.

rubrics_metrics.name: prisoner-of-war hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a compound modifier: 'prisoner-of-war camp' (hyphenate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow hyphenation for compound modifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: pristine meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Pristine means belonging to the earliest period or in its original state, not just clean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid loose use meaning simply 'very clean'.

rubrics_metrics.name: prize money
rubrics_metrics.description: Two words: 'prize money'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use two-word form.

rubrics_metrics.name: private equity firm
rubrics_metrics.description: Three words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'private equity firm' as three separate words.

rubrics_metrics.name: privilege / privileged spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not spell 'privileged' as 'priviledged'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct spelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: proactive word choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'active' or 'energetic' instead of 'proactive'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clearer, less jargonistic terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: process verbosity
rubrics_metrics.description: The noun 'process' can usually be excised in phrases such as 'development process'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer more direct phrasing and active words.

rubrics_metrics.name: company/proper-name spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the style and spelling as it appears on the organisation’s own nameplate and business cards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Scottish Labour Party, U.S. Department of Defense. When proper names are translated into English use the regional spelling convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: prognosis definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Prognosis is forecasting, or a forecast, especially of a disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use in correct medical/forecasting context.

rubrics_metrics.name: program vs programme spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'program' only in stories about computers and for stock market program trading; otherwise 'programme' (British). In American style, 'program' is for all uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow regional and topical conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: pro-life terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'anti-abortion' instead of 'pro-life'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clear, descriptive terminology over advocacy labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: pronouns for objects/collectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Use neuter pronouns for countries, ships, cars, aircraft, animals, etc. (e.g. Portugal and its territories; aboard the liner when it sailed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasional gendered pronoun for machines/animals may be used rarely for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: pronunciation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: For difficult personal or place names, provide a pronunciation guide on first appearance for radio/TV subscribers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyphenate syllables and capitalise stressed syllable in brackets after the name, e.g. General Michel Aoun (pronounced OW-oon). Assume familiarity with European-language pronunciation principles and do not provide guides for most names transcribed from another script.

rubrics_metrics.name: proper names styling
rubrics_metrics.description: If proper names are in English use the style and spelling as on the organisation’s own nameplate; if translated into English use the region's spelling convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow organisations' own usage for official names (e.g., Centers for Disease Control and Prevention).

rubrics_metrics.name: proscribe vs prescribe
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribe means to prohibit; prescribe to set down as an order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct verb.

rubrics_metrics.name: prostate vs prostrate
rubrics_metrics.description: Prostate is a gland; prostrate means lying face down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse the terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: protest usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'protest against a government' or 'protest about a policy'; if it is a solemn declaration rather than disapproval use 'protest the faith' or 'protest his innocence'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write 'a protest' when describing a demonstration; American style drops the adverb for the verb of disapproval ('protest the policy').

rubrics_metrics.name: protester vs protestor
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'protester' not 'protestor'; consider 'demonstrator' as alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer standard noun forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: prototype usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Prototype means the original model; do not qualify with 'first prototype' or 'an early prototype'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid redundant modifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: proved vs proven
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'proved' generally; exceptions: writing of oil reserves or of the Scottish legal verdict 'not proven'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'proved' except in specified contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: proverbial
rubrics_metrics.description: Best excised; if you are using or describing a proverb there is no need to say 'proverbial'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary qualifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: public school
rubrics_metrics.description: In some countries 'public school' refers to a private fee-paying school; use only when quoting someone and then explain it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify non-obvious local meanings for international readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: publications formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: No quotation marks around the title of publications; capitalise articles and particles in names of English-language newspapers and magazines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-English newspapers that begin with a word meaning 'the', write the name without adding 'the' (e.g., O Globo, Le Monde, Die Welt).

rubrics_metrics.name: publicly spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell 'publicly' (not 'publically').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct spelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: pull back / pullback
rubrics_metrics.description: Two words for the verb ('pull back'), one for the noun ('pullback').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use forms according to part of speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: pull out / pullout
rubrics_metrics.description: Two words for the verb, one word for the noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As above.

rubrics_metrics.name: punctuation: apostrophes
rubrics_metrics.description: Singular words and plurals not ending in s form the possessive by adding '’s'. Plural words already ending in s form the possessive by adding the apostrophe alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable to use ’s with words ending in s if pronunciation is easy (class’s performance); avoid ugly constructions (Dukakises' son) by recasting the phrase. Note 'it's' is contraction for 'it is'; possessive of it is 'its'. Do not use apostrophe in '1990s' or abbreviations like 'NCOs'.

rubrics_metrics.name: punctuation: brackets
rubrics_metrics.description: If an entire sentence is in brackets, put the full stop inside the closing bracket. If a sentence has a bracketed section at the end, the full stop goes outside the closing bracket. A bracketed section in the middle of a sentence followed by a comma also goes outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow placement rules to preserve sentence punctuation clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: punctuation: colons
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a colon before directly quoting a complete sentence and to introduce a list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put the word following a colon in lower case unless it is a proper name, direct quotation or the start of a sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: punctuation: commas
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not over-punctuate, especially with commas. Use commas to guide sense and separate logically discrete parts, mark off apposition and non-essential clauses, and separate list items. Normally there is no comma before the final 'and' unless needed for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comma follows an initial 'however'; opening phrases like 'On Wednesday the committee decided ...' generally need no comma unless ambiguity arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: punctuation: dashes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dashes sparingly, never to set off relative clauses. Dashes should be double (–) and hyphens single (-). Dashes are followed by lower case unless used to label list sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example list formatting provided in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: hyphenation general rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use hyphen if omission might lead to ambiguity (e.g., 'three-year-old horses' vs 'three year-old horses'). Hyphens show words read together as single unit; many former hyphenated words now closed; hyphenate adjectives forming compound modifiers, paired adjectives making single adjective, fractions, secondary compass points (south-southwest), and certain noun pairs; do not hyphenate adverb-adjective pairs when adverb ends in -ly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyphenate where omission causes ambiguity, when forming compound modifiers before nouns, and follow numerous listed exceptions (pre-/re- before e, non- negative, titles like under-secretary). Hyphenate both terms in short- and medium-range forms. Ensure consistency in conversions with hyphenation.

rubrics_metrics.name: punter usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'gambler' not 'bettor'; do not use 'punter' in financial stories as a synonym for investors or speculators unless in quotes (then explain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid regional slang that may confuse international readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: purchase phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'buy' as it is shorter and better than 'purchase'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concise verbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: push up / push-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Two words for the verb ('push up'), one word for the noun ('push-up').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As with other verb/noun forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: pygmy capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower case 'pygmy' when meaning small (pygmy hippopotamus); upper case for members of specific human groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize appropriately depending on meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pyrrhic victory
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition: a victory at great cost to the victor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use term with its proper meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: quotations (general principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotes are sacred: do not alter anything in quotation marks other than to delete words, and only if the deletion does not alter the sense. Quotes personalise stories and give immediacy; try to inject a quote into the first three paragraphs where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before starting a quote, use a colon. Delete routine obscenities. Show deletions with three full stops with a space before and after. If omitted words are at the end of a sentence followed by another sentence in quotes, capitalise the next word. Background or explanation of a quote should be a separate paragraph or bracketing a phrase into the quoted remarks. When quoting the same source at length, do not need to repeat the source paragraph by paragraph if it's clear who is speaking. Do not run one person's quote into another's—use bridging sentences. Avoid quotes in colloquial/parochial language without explanation; when translating quotes idiomatically prefer idiomatic English but provide literal translation when tendentious. Avoid excessive direct quotes in English when the speaker spoke another language. Spell out what is actually spoken rather than using customary style abbreviations in quotes (e.g., write 'Doctor' not 'Dr' if that's what was spoken). Quote titles of films, plays and books but not of ships, aircraft, newspapers or magazines.

rubrics_metrics.name: quotations: punctuation with quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Full stop (period) placement depends on whether the quotation is a complete sentence or the final part of the sentence; commas after quoted clauses depend on position of quotation and sentence structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: full stop goes inside quotation marks when the quotation is a complete sentence; it goes outside when the quotation is the final part of the sentence. When the quotation precedes the source put the comma inside the quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: race reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reuters stories should be free of conscious or unconscious racism. Avoid racial stereotyping and describe membership of a group, ethnicity or race precisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention race/ethnicity only when relevant to understanding the story (e.g., deportation, racial threats). Take care in reporting crimes and court cases — race of accused usually not relevant. Use the term people use for themselves (Inuit not Eskimo, Roma not Gypsy). Capitalise names of races and peoples (Asian, Jew, Hispanic); 'black' and 'white' are lower case. If a racial slur appears in a direct quote flag it at the top of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red Cross naming and first reference
rubrics_metrics.description: The Red Cross movement comprises the ICRC, the International Federation (IFRC) and national societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the ICRC title in full at first reference; do not abbreviate to 'International Red Cross'. For brevity in a lead you can refer to a Red Cross official or spokesman but make clear lower in the story which organisation he belongs to. See official websites for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: re- prefix hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the second element of a word beginning with re- starts with an e, hyphenate (e.g., re-employ, re-elected).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow hyphenation when necessary for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: reassure usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'reassure' with caution — it means to give a new assurance, not necessarily that the person is thereby reassured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'again assured' in contexts where that meaning is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: rebut / refute usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Refute means to disprove, not to deny or reject; rebut has a similar meaning and implies editorial judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'refute' or 'rebut' except in quotes or where certain of the meaning; prefer 'deny' or 'reject' if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: recession definition (US)
rubrics_metrics.description: A period of low economic activity with high unemployment and numerous business failures; in the US often defined as two consecutive quarterly falls in GDP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of differing definitions in different jurisdictions.
